paragraphs: Certain subjects absorb our entire interest, yet are altogether too horrible for acceptable fiction. A writer of invented tales must avoid them unless he wishes to offend or disgust. They can properly be handled only when the stern grandeur of Truth makes them sacred and sustains them. For example, we feel the most intense “pleasurable pain” when reading accounts of the Passage of the Beresina, the Earthquake at Lisbon, the Plague at London, the Massacre of St Bartholomew, or the suffocation of the hundred and twenty-three prisoners in the Black Hole at Calcutta. But in these accounts it is the fact—it is the reality—it is the history that excites us. If they were invented, we would regard them with nothing but horror and disgust.

I have named a few of the most notable and awe-inspiring calamities on record. Yet their scale, no less than their nature, is what so vividly impresses the imagination. I need hardly remind the reader that, from the long and strange catalogue of human misery, I could have chosen many individual cases containing more actual suffering than any of these sweeping accounts of disaster. True wretchedness—the deepest sorrow—is individual, not spread among many. The ghastliest extremes of agony are endured by a single human being, never by humanity as a mass. For that, let us thank a merciful God!

To be buried alive is unquestionably the most terrifying of these extremes ever suffered by a mortal. Few thoughtful people will deny that it has happened often—very often. At best, the boundaries between Life and Death are shadowy and vague. Who can say where one ends and the other begins? We know there are diseases in which every apparent function of life stops completely, yet is only suspended. These are temporary pauses in an incomprehensible mechanism. Some time passes, and an unseen, mysterious force sets the magical gears and enchanted wheels moving again. The silver cord was not loosened for ever, nor the golden bowl broken beyond repair. But where, meanwhile, was the soul?

Reasoning alone leads inevitably to one conclusion: such causes must produce such effects. Known cases of suspended animation must naturally lead, now and then, to burial before death. But apart from that reasoning, we have direct testimony from medical and everyday experience proving that a vast number of such burials have occurred. If necessary, I could immediately cite a hundred well-authenticated cases. A particularly remarkable one happened not long ago in the neighbouring city of Baltimore. Some readers may still remember the circumstances, which caused painful, intense and widespread excitement. The wife of one of its most respected citizens, a prominent lawyer and member of Congress, was struck by a sudden, unexplained illness that completely baffled her doctors. After much suffering, she died—or was thought to have died. No one suspected, or had reason to suspect, that she was not truly dead. She showed all the usual signs. Her face took on the familiar pinched, sunken shape. Her lips had the usual marble paleness. Her eyes were dull. There was no warmth. Her pulse had stopped. The body was kept unburied for three days, during which it became rigid as stone. In short, the funeral was hurried because what was thought to be decomposition was advancing rapidly.

The woman was placed in her family vault, which remained undisturbed for the next three years. At the end of that time, it was opened to receive a sarcophagus. But alas, what a dreadful shock awaited her husband, who opened the door himself! As it swung outwards, something dressed in white fell rattling into his arms. It was his wife’s skeleton, still wrapped in a shroud that had not yet mouldered.

Careful investigation made it clear that she had revived within two days of being placed in the tomb. Her struggles inside the coffin had knocked it from a ledge or shelf to the floor, breaking it enough for her to escape. A lamp, accidentally left full of oil in the tomb, was found empty. The oil might, however, have evaporated. On the outermost step leading down into that dreadful chamber lay a large piece of the coffin. It seemed she had used it to strike the iron door and attract attention. While doing so, she probably fainted, or perhaps died of sheer terror. As she fell, her shroud caught in some ironwork projecting inwards. There she remained, and there she rotted, upright.

In 1810, a case of burial alive occurred in France under circumstances that go far towards proving that truth is indeed stranger than fiction. The story’s heroine was Miss Victorine Lafourcade, a young woman from a distinguished family, wealthy and very beautiful. Among her many suitors was Julien Bossuet, a poor writer or journalist from Paris. His talents and generally pleasant nature had attracted the heiress’s attention, and she seems to have truly loved him. But pride in her birth finally led her to reject him and marry Mr Renelle, a banker and diplomat of some prominence. After their marriage he neglected her and perhaps actively mistreated her too. After several miserable years with him, she died—or at least her condition resembled death so closely that everyone who saw her was deceived. She was buried, not in a vault, but in an ordinary grave in her native village. Despairing, and still burning with the memory of his profound love, Bossuet travels from the capital to the remote province where the village stands. His romantic purpose is to dig up her body and take possession of her luxuriant hair. He reaches the grave. At midnight he unearths the coffin, opens it, and is cutting off the hair when the beloved eyes open and stop him. She had, in fact, been buried alive. Life had not entirely left her, and her lover’s caresses roused her from the stupor mistaken for death. Frantically he carried her to his lodgings in the village. With considerable medical knowledge, he used powerful restoratives. In short, she revived. She recognised her rescuer and stayed with him while she slowly regained all her former health. Her woman’s heart was not made of stone, and this last lesson in love softened it enough for her to give it to Bossuet. She never returned to her husband. Keeping her return to life secret from him, she fled with her lover to America. Twenty years later they returned to France, believing time had changed her appearance so much that her friends would not recognise her. They were wrong. At their very first meeting, Mr Renelle recognised his wife and claimed her back. She resisted, and a court upheld her refusal. It ruled that the unusual circumstances and the long passage of years had ended her husband’s authority, not only in fairness but in law.

The “Chirurgical Journal” of Leipsic is a periodical of great authority and merit, which some American bookseller would do well to translate and republish. In a recent issue, it records a deeply distressing event of this kind.

An artillery officer, a huge man in robust health, was thrown from an uncontrollable horse. A severe blow to the head knocked him unconscious at once. His skull was slightly fractured, but no immediate danger was feared. An operation to open the skull was performed successfully. The doctors let blood from him and tried many other usual treatments. Gradually, however, he sank into an increasingly hopeless stupor. At last they thought he had died.

The weather was warm, and he was buried with indecent haste in a public cemetery. The funeral took place on Thursday. On the following Sunday, the cemetery was, as usual, crowded with visitors. Around noon there was intense excitement when a peasant declared that, while sitting on the officer’s grave, he had distinctly felt the earth move, as though someone were struggling beneath it. At first few people paid attention to his claim. But his obvious terror and stubborn insistence finally had their natural effect on the crowd. Spades were hurriedly found. The grave was shamefully shallow, and within a few minutes enough earth had been removed to reveal the occupant’s head. He appeared dead then, but was sitting almost upright in his coffin. In his furious struggles, he had partly raised the lid.

He was immediately taken to the nearest hospital. There he was pronounced still alive, though in a state of suffocation. After some hours he revived, recognised people he knew, and spoke in broken sentences about his agonies in the grave.

His account made it clear that he must have been conscious for more than an hour while buried, before losing awareness again. The grave had been filled carelessly and loosely with very porous soil, so some air had necessarily got through. He heard the crowd’s footsteps overhead and tried in turn to make himself heard. The commotion in the cemetery seemed to have woken him from a deep sleep, he said. But the moment he woke, he fully understood the awful horror of his position.

According to the record, the patient was doing well and seemed likely to recover completely. But he became a victim of quack medical experiments. A galvanic battery was applied, and he suddenly died in one of the violent seizures it sometimes produces.

Yet mention of the galvanic battery reminds me of another well-known and extraordinary case. Here its action restored life to a young London lawyer who had been buried for two days. This happened in 1831 and caused a profound sensation wherever it was discussed.

The patient, Mr Edward Stapleton, had apparently died of typhus fever, with some unusual symptoms that aroused his doctors’ curiosity. After his apparent death, his friends were asked to allow a post-mortem examination, but refused. As often happens after such refusals, the doctors decided to dig up the body and dissect it privately at their leisure. They easily arranged this with members of one of London’s many gangs of body-snatchers. On the third night after the funeral, the supposed corpse was dug from a grave eight feet deep and taken to the dissection room of a private hospital.

A sizeable incision had actually been made in the abdomen when the body’s fresh, undecayed appearance prompted them to try the battery. Experiment followed experiment. The usual effects appeared, with nothing remarkable about them except that, once or twice, the convulsive movements looked more lifelike than usual.

It grew late. Dawn was approaching, and at last they thought it best to begin the dissection immediately. One student, however, particularly wanted to test a theory of his own. He insisted on applying the battery to one of the chest muscles. A rough gash was made, and a wire was hurriedly brought into contact. Then the patient rose from the table with a hurried movement entirely unlike a convulsion. He stepped into the middle of the floor, looked around uneasily for a few seconds, and then—spoke. No one could understand what he said, but he uttered words, their syllables clearly formed. After speaking, he fell heavily to the floor.

For a few moments everyone was paralysed with awe. But the urgency of the situation soon restored their composure. They saw that Mr Stapleton was alive, although he had fainted. When ether was administered, he revived. He quickly regained his health and returned to his friends. However, they were not told that he had been brought back to life until there was no longer any fear of a relapse. Their wonder—their ecstatic astonishment—can be imagined.

The most thrilling feature of this incident, however, lies in Mr S.’s own account. He says he was never completely unconscious. Dimly and confusedly, he knew everything that happened to him, from the moment his doctors pronounced him dead until he fainted onto the hospital floor. When he recognised the dissection room, the words he had struggled to utter in his desperate state, but which no one understood, were “I am alive.”

It would be easy to add more accounts like these, but I refrain. We do not need them to establish that premature burials happen. Given the nature of such cases, we very rarely have the power to discover them. We must therefore admit that they may often occur without our knowledge. Indeed, hardly any graveyard is substantially disturbed for any purpose without revealing skeletons in positions that suggest the most dreadful suspicions.

Dreadful indeed is the suspicion—but more dreadful the fate! Without hesitation, we may say that nothing is better suited to cause the utmost physical and mental anguish than burial before death. The unbearable pressure on the lungs; the suffocating fumes of damp earth; clinging to the burial clothes; the rigid embrace of the narrow house; the blackness of absolute Night; the silence that overwhelms like a sea; the unseen yet tangible presence of the Conqueror Worm. Add thoughts of the air and grass above, memories of dear friends who would rush to save us if they knew our fate, and the knowledge that they can never be told—that our hopeless lot is the same as that of the truly dead. These thoughts bring such appalling, intolerable horror into the still-beating heart that even the boldest imagination must recoil. Nothing on Earth is so agonising. In the depths of the lowest Hell, we can imagine nothing half so hideous. Every account of this subject therefore holds a profound interest. Yet, because of the subject’s sacred terror, that interest very properly depends, in a special way, on our belief that the account is true. What I now have to tell comes from my own certain knowledge, my own definite and personal experience.

For several years I had suffered attacks of the strange disorder doctors have agreed to call catalepsy, for lack of a more definite name. Its immediate causes, the things that predispose a person to it, and even its actual diagnosis remain mysterious. But its visible, apparent character is well enough understood. Its variations seem mainly to be differences of degree. Sometimes a patient lies for just a day, or less, in a kind of extreme stupor. He has no awareness and makes no outward movement. Yet the heartbeat can still be faintly detected, some warmth remains, and a little colour lingers in the centre of the cheek. If a mirror is held to his lips, we can detect sluggish, uneven and wavering breathing. At other times the trance lasts weeks, even months. The closest examination and strictest medical tests fail to reveal any substantial difference between his condition and what we consider absolute death. Usually only his friends’ knowledge that he has suffered catalepsy before, the suspicion that knowledge arouses, and above all the absence of decay save him from premature burial. Fortunately, the illness develops gradually. Its first signs, though noticeable, are unmistakable. The fits become more and more distinctive, each lasting longer than the previous one. This is the main protection against burial. An unfortunate person whose first attack took the extreme form sometimes seen would almost inevitably be sent alive to the tomb.

My own case differed in no important way from those described in medical books. Sometimes, without any apparent cause, I slowly sank into a state of partial fainting, or a half-faint. I had no pain, could not move or, strictly speaking, think. Yet I retained a dull, sluggish awareness of being alive and of the people around my bed. I stayed that way until the illness reached its turning point and suddenly restored me to full sensation. At other times I was struck swiftly and violently. I felt sick, numb, cold and dizzy, and immediately collapsed. Then, for weeks, everything was empty, black and silent. Nothing became the universe. Complete annihilation could be no more. From these attacks, however, I woke as slowly as they had begun suddenly. Day dawns upon a friendless, homeless beggar who has wandered the streets throughout a long, desolate winter night. Just as slowly, just as wearily, just as cheerfully, the light of the Soul returned to me.

Apart from these trances, my general health seemed good. I could not see that the recurring illness affected it at all, unless it also caused a peculiarity of my ordinary sleep. On waking, I could never immediately recover full use of my senses. For many minutes I remained bewildered and confused. My mental powers in general, and especially my memory, were completely suspended.

Throughout all this I suffered no physical pain, but my mental anguish was boundless. My imagination filled with tombs. I spoke “of worms, of tombs, and epitaphs.” I lost myself in thoughts of death, and the idea of being buried alive possessed my mind continually. The ghastly Danger that threatened me haunted me day and night. By day, the torment of thinking about it was excessive; at night, it was supreme. When grim Darkness spread over the Earth, every horrifying thought made me shake—shake like the quivering plumes on a hearse. When my body could stay awake no longer, I surrendered to sleep only after a struggle. I shuddered to think that I might wake to find myself occupying a grave. When I finally fell asleep, I rushed at once into a world of phantoms. Above it all hovered that one thought of the tomb, dominant, with its vast, black, overshadowing wing.

Of the countless gloomy images that oppressed my dreams, I choose to record just one vision. I seemed to be deep in a cataleptic trance, longer and more profound than usual. Suddenly an icy hand touched my forehead. An impatient, gibbering voice whispered in my ear, “Get up!”

I sat upright. The darkness was complete. I could not see the figure that had woken me. I could remember neither when I had fallen into the trance nor where I was lying. While I remained still, trying to gather my thoughts, the cold hand gripped my wrist fiercely and shook it impatiently. The gibbering voice spoke again:
“Get up! Didn’t I tell you to get up?”
“And who,” I demanded, “are you?”

“I have no name in the regions where I live,” the voice replied mournfully. “I was mortal, but now I am a fiend. I was merciless, but now I am full of pity. You can feel me shuddering. My teeth chatter as I speak, but not from the cold of the night—the night without end. This horror is unbearable. How can you sleep peacefully? I cannot rest because of the cries of these great agonies. These sights are more than I can bear. Get up! Come with me into the outer Night, and let me open the graves to your sight. Is this not a spectacle of misery? Look!”

I looked. The unseen figure, still gripping my wrist, had caused the graves of all humanity to open. From each came the faint, phosphorescent glow of decay. I could see into their deepest recesses and look at the shrouded bodies in their sad, solemn sleep beside the worm. But alas, by many millions, fewer truly slept than did not sleep at all. There was feeble struggling, and a widespread, sorrowful restlessness. From the depths of countless pits came the mournful rustling of the buried people’s clothes. Among those who seemed to rest peacefully, I saw that vast numbers had moved, a little or a great deal, from the stiff, uncomfortable positions in which they had been buried. As I gazed, the voice spoke again:

“Is it not—oh, is it not a pitiful sight?” Before I could find words to reply, the figure released my wrist, the phosphorescent lights died, and the graves slammed shut. From them rose a clamour of despairing cries, saying again, “Is it not—oh God, is it not a very pitiful sight?”

Night-time visions like these extended their terrifying influence far into my waking hours. My nerves were completely shattered, and I became a prey to constant horror. I hesitated to ride, walk or take any exercise that would lead me away from home. In fact, I no longer dared leave the immediate presence of people who knew I was prone to catalepsy. I feared an ordinary attack might lead to my burial before my real condition was discovered. I doubted the care and loyalty of my dearest friends. I dreaded that, during an unusually long trance, they might be persuaded I could never recover. I even feared that, because I caused so much trouble, they might welcome a prolonged attack as an excuse to be rid of me altogether. Their most solemn promises could not reassure me. I demanded sacred oaths that they would never bury me, under any circumstances, until decay had advanced so far that keeping me any longer was impossible. Even then, my mortal terrors would listen to no reason and accept no comfort. I took a series of elaborate precautions. Among other things, I had the family vault altered so it could easily be opened from inside. The lightest pressure on a long lever reaching far into the tomb would make the iron door fly open. I also arranged for air and light to enter freely, and placed convenient containers for food and water within easy reach of my intended coffin. The coffin had warm, soft padding. Its lid worked on the same principle as the vault door, with additional springs arranged so that the body’s faintest movement would be enough to free it. Besides all this, a large bell hung from the tomb’s roof. Its rope was intended to pass through a hole in the coffin and be tied to one of the corpse’s hands. But alas, what use is vigilance against human Destiny? Even these carefully designed safeguards could not save a wretch already doomed to them from the utmost agonies of being buried alive!

A time came, as it had often come before, when I found myself emerging from total unconsciousness into the first faint, uncertain sense of existence. Slowly, at a tortoise’s pace, the pale grey dawn of the mind’s day approached. A sluggish uneasiness. A numb endurance of dull pain. No concern—no hope—no effort. Then, after a long interval, ringing in the ears. After a still longer interval, a prickling or tingling in the hands and feet. Then a seemingly endless stretch of pleasant stillness, while the waking feelings struggle to become thought. Then a brief sinking back into nothingness. Then a sudden recovery. At last, the faint trembling of an eyelid, followed immediately by the electric shock of a deadly, undefined terror that sends blood pouring from the temples to the heart. Now the first definite effort to think. Now the first attempt to remember. Now a partial, fleeting success. Now memory has regained enough control for me to understand something of my condition. I feel that I am not waking from ordinary sleep. I remember that I have suffered catalepsy. Now, at last, as if beneath the rush of an ocean, my shuddering spirit is overwhelmed by the one grim Danger, the one ghostly thought that is always present.

For several minutes after this thought seized me, I did not move. Why? I could not find the courage. I dared not make the effort that would reveal my fate, although something in my heart whispered that it was certain. After a long hesitation, despair alone urged me to raise my heavy eyelids—despair such as no other misery can create. I raised them. It was dark—all dark. I knew the fit was over. I knew the crisis of my illness had long passed. I knew my sight had fully returned. Yet it was dark—all dark—the intense, utterly lightless Night that lasts for ever.

I tried to scream. My lips and dry tongue moved convulsively together in the attempt, but no voice came from my hollow lungs. They seemed crushed beneath the weight of a mountain. With every laborious, struggling breath, they gasped and throbbed along with my heart.

Moving my jaws as I tried to cry out, I discovered they were bound up, as is customary with the dead. I also felt that I lay on something hard, with something similar pressing tightly against my sides. Until then I had not dared move any limb. Now I violently flung up my arms, which had been lying outstretched with the wrists crossed. They struck solid wood extending over me no more than six inches from my face. I could no longer doubt that I lay inside a coffin at last.

Now, amid all my boundless misery, the cherub Hope came sweetly to me. I remembered my precautions. I writhed and struggled in spasms to force open the lid. It would not move. I felt around my wrists for the bell rope. It was not there. Then the Comforter fled for ever, and a still harsher Despair reigned in triumph. I could not help noticing the absence of the padding I had so carefully prepared. Then, suddenly, the strong, distinctive smell of damp earth reached my nostrils. The conclusion was unavoidable. I was not in the vault. I had fallen into a trance away from home, among strangers. I could not remember when or how. They had buried me like a dog, nailed inside an ordinary coffin, and thrust deep, deep and for ever into an ordinary, nameless grave.

As this terrible conviction forced its way into the deepest chambers of my soul, I again struggled to cry out. This time I succeeded. A long, wild, unbroken scream—a yell of agony—echoed through the realms of the underground Night.
“Hello! Hello there!” a gruff voice answered.
“What the devil’s the matter now?” said a second.
“Get out of there!” said a third.

“What do you mean, yowling like that, like a wildcat?” said a fourth. Then a group of very rough-looking men seized me and shook me unceremoniously for several minutes. They did not wake me from sleep, for I had been wide awake when I screamed. But they fully restored my memory.

This adventure happened near Richmond, Virginia. With a friend, I had gone on a shooting expedition some miles down the banks of the James River. Night was coming, and a storm overtook us. Our only shelter was the cabin of a small sloop anchored in the river and loaded with garden soil. We made the best of it and spent the night aboard. I slept in one of the vessel’s only two berths. The berths of a sloop of sixty or twenty tons hardly need describing. Mine had no bedding of any kind. At its widest it measured eighteen inches, and the distance from its bottom to the deck above was exactly the same. Squeezing into it was extremely difficult. Nevertheless, I slept soundly. The whole of my vision—for it was neither a dream nor a nightmare—arose naturally from my circumstances, my usual habits of thought, and the difficulty I have already described in recovering my senses, especially my memory, for a long time after waking. The men who shook me were the sloop’s crew and some labourers hired to unload it. The earthy smell came from its cargo. The binding around my jaws was a silk handkerchief I had tied around my head because I lacked my usual nightcap.

For the time they lasted, however, my torments were undoubtedly as great as those of an actual burial. They were hideous—terribly, unimaginably hideous. Yet Good came from Evil. Their very excess inevitably made my spirit recoil against them. My soul gained strength, gained resilience. I went abroad. I took vigorous exercise. I breathed the free air of Heaven. I thought about subjects other than Death. I threw away my medical books. “Buchan” I burned. I read no “Night Thoughts,” no pompous writing about churchyards, no bogeyman tales—such as this one. In short, I became a new man and lived a man’s life. From that memorable night onwards, I banished my fears of the tomb for ever. With them vanished the cataleptic disorder, of which perhaps they had been less the result than the cause.

There are moments when, even to Reason’s sober eye, the world of our sorrowful Humanity can resemble Hell. But the human imagination is no Carathis, free to explore every cavern without harm. Alas, the grim army of terrors from the tomb cannot be dismissed as entirely imaginary. But like the Demons who travelled with Afrasiab down the Oxus, they must sleep, or they will devour us. They must be allowed to slumber, or we perish.
